video_title: Capital Efficiency Is the Next Edge | Open Interest | Ep.23
gist: Moritz Seibert interviews Charlie McGara, CIO of Altus Partners (a trend-following CTA turned ETF subadvisor), on his path from Goldman metals trading through sports betting and blockchain.com to acquiring Altus, and on his core theses: that the regime shift from volatility-suppressing QE to volatility-inducing geopolitics favors adaptive systematic strategies, that capital efficiency and prudent leverage sizing (via Kelly-criterion thinking) matter more than most investors realize, and that Chinese onshore commodity futures offer a genuinely independent, structurally distinct source of diversification.

themes.theme: Career arc: from Goldman metals trading to CTA subadvisor

insights.claim: Charlie McGara left Goldman Sachs in 2016 to build a sports-betting analytics business explicitly as a vehicle to gain hands-on machine-learning and data-science experience, later acknowledging that being early to a trend can be functionally indistinguishable from being wrong.
insights.speaker: Charlie McGara
insights.so_what: A useful caution for investors evaluating early-stage thematic bets (like early ML/AI adoption plays): being conceptually right ahead of the market can still produce a losing outcome if timing is off.
insights.quote: like many things in my life, early is the same thing as wrong

insights.claim: McGara's sports-betting business was sold to blockchain.com in 2018 essentially as an 'aqua-hire' -- the buyer valued the team's software-engineering and trading-systems capability rather than the sports-betting book itself, illustrating how quantitative/engineering talent and tooling can be repackaged across seemingly unrelated verticals (sports betting into crypto trading).
insights.speaker: Charlie McGara
insights.so_what: A concrete data point on how M&A in adjacent-but-different verticals (betting/prediction markets to crypto) is often really talent/infrastructure acquisition, relevant to valuing similar cross-vertical fintech acquisitions.
insights.quote: it was it was more of an aqua hire

insights.claim: McGara acquired his stake in Altus Partners in March 2020, right as COVID hit, after the firm's co-founder died in a skiing avalanche in 2019 -- judging that Altus's trend-following and portfolio-construction IP, built since 2000, was directly transferable to leveraged trading in crypto and traditional futures alike.
insights.speaker: Charlie McGara
insights.so_what: Illustrates a thesis that generic systematic trend/portfolio-construction IP is asset-class agnostic and can be redeployed across futures, crypto, and other levered instruments -- relevant when assessing the portability of a systematic manager's edge into new markets.

themes.theme: The regime shift: from volatility suppression to volatility inducement

insights.claim: McGara argues that the QE era of roughly 2010-2019, in which governments globally suppressed volatility with cheap, low-velocity liquidity, was structurally hostile to trend-following returns; but since Brexit and Trump's first term, government policy (tariffs, trade wars, geopolitical conflict) has flipped to actively inducing volatility, which favors adaptive, reactive systematic strategies over static or passive ones.
insights.speaker: Charlie McGara
insights.so_what: A macro regime-change thesis directly favoring trend-following/CTA and other adaptive systematic strategies over buy-and-hold passive allocation for the foreseeable future -- relevant to tactical allocation between passive and systematic-active exposures.
insights.quote: now the government's in the business of volatility inducement right starting wars trade policy tariff you name it

insights.claim: McGara estimates that roughly 60% of market flows behave as effectively zero-reactivity passive capital (pure dollar-cost-averaging) that structurally never updates its views regardless of new information, which he frames as one extreme of a design spectrum whose opposite extreme (maximal reactivity) bleeds out on transaction costs and overfitting -- with genuinely adaptive-but-cost-aware strategies occupying an underexploited middle ground.
insights.speaker: Charlie McGara
insights.so_what: Quantifies how much of total market capital is structurally unresponsive to new information, implying a persistent opportunity for well-costed adaptive strategies to extract value from that inertia, especially as fundamental volatility rises.
insights.quote: something like 60% of the market is on that theory of the case

themes.theme: Capital efficiency and Kelly-criterion position sizing

insights.claim: McGara argues futures markets are uniquely capital-efficient because they give ordinary allocators access to synthetic leverage/funding at rates close to what banks themselves obtain -- a form of 'dynamic leverage' he believes the CTA industry has historically undersold relative to its emphasis on pure alpha generation.
insights.speaker: Charlie McGara
insights.so_what: Reframes managed-futures/CTA products' value proposition around capital-efficient leverage access rather than just return generation -- relevant to how such products should be marketed and compared against margin-account alternatives.
insights.quote: it's kind of like the only way that normal people can get access to borrowing as cheap as like a bank can just synthetically

insights.claim: McGara states that the incremental compounded-return benefit of tolerating a larger drawdown (e.g., a 20-point vs. a 10-point drawdown) is highly nonlinear and far larger than the proportional difference in the drawdown itself once time horizon is factored in, making drawdown tolerance and position sizing a more important lever for long-run compounded returns than most investors appreciate relative to alpha generation.
insights.speaker: Charlie McGara
insights.so_what: A high-conviction, quantifiable insight for portfolio construction: investors and allocators should spend as much analytical effort on sizing/drawdown tolerance as on predicting returns, since the payoff to increased risk tolerance compounds nonlinearly.
insights.quote: the difference between somebody who can live with, you know, a 10-point draw down versus somebody who can live with a 20 point draw down is not like 10% more. It's like it's like way bigger than that depending on your time horizon.

insights.claim: McGara invokes the Kelly criterion to argue that betting above full Kelly is destructive under estimation error and that even full Kelly requires high confidence in one's return-distribution estimates -- but in systematic futures trading, unlike sports betting, there are no clearly defined odds, making fractional-Kelly position sizing an inherently imprecise, judgment-based exercise rather than a formula-driven one.
insights.speaker: Charlie McGara
insights.so_what: A grounded caution against over-mechanizing position-sizing models in strategies without well-defined payoff distributions -- relevant to how quant funds should calibrate leverage versus the false precision of a Kelly-derived number.
insights.quote: even you know coming up with a fractional Kelly is kind of like ... it's not a precise exercise

insights.claim: McGara distinguishes retail-style leverage products (e.g., 3x leveraged single-stock/index ETPs) which he says are effectively 'sentenced to death by volatility drag,' from prudent, diversified capital-efficiency strategies that he believes represent an underexploited 'efficient frontier' opportunity for asset managers to package for clients.
insights.speaker: Charlie McGara
insights.so_what: Draws a sharp product-quality line between naive leveraged retail products (structurally value-destructive) and diversified, actively risk-managed leverage -- relevant for distinguishing 'good' from 'bad' leveraged product design in the current ETF boom.
insights.quote: it's like gambling product that that is sentenced to death by volatility drag basically

themes.theme: Altus's Enhanced Macro program and the trend-following business

insights.claim: Altus's core trend-following program trades roughly 150 markets across equities, fixed income (STIR), FX, and commodities globally, and its newer 'Enhanced Macro' program layers additional factor-based return-prediction systems (value/carry/reversion-style) on top of the same long-standing portfolio-construction IP rather than replacing trend with something new.
insights.speaker: Charlie McGara
insights.so_what: Gives investors a concrete picture of the strategy's breadth (150 markets, multi-asset) and evolution (trend plus blended factors), useful for comparing Altus's offering against pure-trend CTA peers.
insights.quote: we're trading something like 150ish markets across many many regulated exchanges all over the world

insights.claim: McGara states trend-following performed poorly through the 2010s specifically because QE-driven volatility suppression was inimical to the trend factor's returns, which forced Altus to refactor its systems by the mid-2010s toward a more multi-dimensional, multi-risk-premia approach rather than relying on pure trend alone.
insights.speaker: Charlie McGara
insights.so_what: Provides a causal mechanism (QE volatility suppression) for the well-known 2010s CTA underperformance period, useful context for assessing whether the current volatility-inducing regime should structurally favor a return to strong trend performance.
insights.quote: the amount of liquidity provided to the government or to the market via QE and the volatility suppression... was just kind of enimical to to the returns of the trend factor

themes.theme: ETF product design, distribution, and the 'product manager' mindset

insights.claim: McGara credits a chance 2021 meeting with Mike Green (a former Goldman client, then at Simplify) at a Bretton Woods macro conference for the decision to launch a managed-futures ETF -- the product went from casual conversation to being listed on a stock exchange within six months.
insights.speaker: Charlie McGara
insights.so_what: Illustrates how quickly institutional trading IP can be repackaged into scalable, retail-distributed ETF product once the right distribution partner and platform appear -- relevant to tracking the pace of similar CTA-to-ETF conversions industry-wide.
insights.quote: 6 months later, you know, we were we were launching product on stock exchange

insights.claim: McGara explicitly imports a 'product manager' mindset from his time in tech and crypto, arguing that how trading IP is packaged (as an uncorrelated absolute-return stream, a statistical hedge, or a contractual/defined-outcome hedge) is as important a design decision as the underlying alpha itself, since different packagings trade off scalability against strategy resolution and complexity.
insights.speaker: Charlie McGara
insights.so_what: A transferable product-design framework for any systematic manager deciding how to wrap proprietary signals into a fund structure (hedge fund/SMA vs. ETF) -- relevant for evaluating why certain CTA strategies choose particular vehicle structures.
insights.quote: being a product manager I think is equally or even more important than being ... a portfolio manager

insights.claim: McGara built the Simplify-subadvised ETFs using Altus's own proprietary signals rather than replicating existing managed-futures/trend ETF products, reasoning that since the underlying strategy is software and thus scalable, someone else would eventually deliver a similar product anyway -- so there was no defensive value in avoiding direct competition with existing replication-style products.
insights.speaker: Charlie McGara
insights.so_what: Reflects a 'race to build, not race to hide' competitive philosophy in the increasingly crowded liquid-alternatives ETF space, relevant to how differentiated any given managed-futures ETF's underlying signal set actually is.
insights.quote: eventually somebody else will deliver it if if they're any good. So we we might as well

insights.claim: McGara predicts that portfolio construction and product selection will increasingly be mediated by machines and recommendation engines performing mean-variance-style optimization rather than by human advisors, meaning liquidity, track-record length, and covariance/correlation properties will matter more on the margin than raw headline returns or brand recognition as 'agentic allocation' grows as a distribution channel.
insights.speaker: Charlie McGara
insights.so_what: A forward-looking distribution thesis: asset managers should optimize product design for machine-driven allocation discovery (liquidity, correlation profile, track record) much like SEO for search engines, not just for human-advisor storytelling.
insights.quote: it's kind of like SEO. It's like you want to build products that that can get picked up by by whatever those software systems are

insights.claim: McGara estimates that roughly half of a financial advisor's real value-add is psychological relationship management (assuaging client anxiety about money), about 30% is tax and estate planning, and only about 20% is actual investment selection and portfolio construction -- and that this last 20% slice is the part increasingly being automated and mediated by software.
insights.speaker: Charlie McGara
insights.so_what: Segments the value chain of financial advice in a way that clarifies which piece of the advisor's job (portfolio construction) is most exposed to software/AI disintermediation versus which pieces (psychology, tax/estate planning) are more durable.
insights.quote: half the job of the adviser is psychotherapist... Another piece of the job I'd say probably 30% is is tax and estate planning... and then there's 20% which is actual like investment selection

themes.theme: The case for a standalone Chinese onshore commodities product

insights.claim: McGara argues China represents roughly a third to a half of the world's overall molecular and energetic (commodity) flows, trades enormous futures volume through small contract sizes, and is heavily policy-driven, with a financial system only loosely interlinked with the West despite deep physical trade ties -- creating a distinct, largely independent source of bets and diversification for a global macro book.
insights.speaker: Charlie McGara
insights.so_what: A concrete diversification thesis for allocators: Chinese onshore commodity exposure offers genuinely independent bets relative to Western macro books precisely because financial (not physical) linkage between the two systems remains shallow.
insights.quote: it's it's order of magnitude a third to half of the just overall molecular and energetic flows of the the human economy on planet earth

insights.claim: McGara's research finds that short-term momentum historically works better in Chinese commodity markets than in Western markets due to differences in market structure, though the duration/persistence of that Chinese momentum factor appears to be extending over time as Chinese markets mature and become incrementally more interlinked with the West.
insights.speaker: Charlie McGara
insights.so_what: A specific, testable factor-research finding relevant to systematic strategy design for China-focused commodity trading -- shorter-wavelength momentum signals may currently be better suited to Chinese markets than longer-wavelength trend signals.
insights.quote: short-term momentum seems to work better in China than it did in in in western markets

insights.claim: McGara argues that a deglobalization impulse (citing recent trade-policy shifts) could just as easily widen the divergence between onshore and offshore Chinese commodity markets as narrow it, framing geopolitical fragmentation itself as a source of tradeable, largely independent bets rather than purely a risk to hedge against.
insights.speaker: Charlie McGara
insights.so_what: Reframes trade-war/deglobalization risk as a potential source of alpha (via onshore/offshore divergence trades) rather than only downside risk -- relevant to how macro funds should think about positioning around further US-China economic fragmentation.
insights.quote: if you get this sort of deglobalization impulse in the system, you might see pretty heavy divergence between onshore and offshore markets and again get some independent bets to make

insights.claim: Altus and Simplify launched a standalone, single-country Chinese onshore commodities ETF rather than blending the exposure into a globally diversified futures program, specifically to give Western allocators concentrated, otherwise hard-to-access exposure -- since accessing these markets typically requires costly, non-frictionless swap arrangements with dealers that McGara wanted to 'unbundle' into a standalone product.
insights.speaker: Charlie McGara
insights.so_what: Explains the product-design rationale behind a specific, identifiable ETF launch (Simplify's Chinese onshore commodities product), relevant to assessing its intended role in an allocator's broader portfolio versus a diversified multi-asset futures product.
insights.quote: if you want a concentrated ability to kind of dial your own exposure in it then then you know here it is
